title: In the gurdwara
hook: no idols, no one seated higher than the Granth, heads covered for all

segments.voice: Yesterday, joining the sangat: the company known by what is said there. Your line was learn together. What did you learn from someone beside you? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

Shoes come off at the door, in long rows on racks. Near the entrance, in some gurdwaras, there's a basket of folded head scarves for anyone who arrived without one. Inside, the hall is mostly floor: carpet or white sheets, and people sitting on it, cross-legged, side by side. There are no pews and no front row of special chairs. At the far end, one thing is raised up, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth. Everything in the room points toward it. Yesterday the code sent a Sikh to the gurdwara. Today it describes the room.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEADS COVERED.` → `A HALL THAT IS MOSTLY FLOOR.` → `ONE THING RAISED UP.`

segments.voice: Gurdwara means the Guru's door. And the Guru, for Sikhs, is the Guru Granth Sahib, the word. So the code arranges the whole room around a single rule, and it shows up three ways. First: no idols. In paraphrase, the code says no idol or image is to be set up in the gurdwara for worship. What Sikhs bow before there is the Guru Granth Sahib, the written word of the Gurus. There's nothing else at the center to look at. Second: no one above the word. The Granth rests on a raised seat under a canopy. The congregation sits on the floor. The code says that sitting on a cushion or a special seat in the Granth's presence, in the sangat, goes against the Guru's way. So a visiting official and the person who swept the hall that morning sit on the same floor, at the same height, facing the same way. The only raised seat in the room belongs to the word. Third: heads covered, for all. Men and women, Sikh or visitor, cover their heads in the Granth's presence. The code also says that any person, of any country, religion or caste, may come into the gurdwara. The door is open. What's asked is the same of everyone who walks through it: shoes off, head covered, sit down on the floor. Put the three together and the room becomes a sentence. Nothing carved stands in for God. No person sits over anyone else. Everyone arrives in the same posture of respect. And in the middle of all of it, raised up and honored, is the word. No one above the word.
screen: `GURDWARA: THE GURU'S DOOR.` · `NO IDOLS; THE WORD AT THE CENTER.` · `NO SEAT HIGHER THAN THE GRANTH.` · `HEADS COVERED; THE DOOR OPEN TO ALL.` · then, large: `NO ONE ABOVE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the gurdwara's order. Settle, and breathe. If you've been inside one, walk through it in your mind: the shoe racks, the scarf on your head, the floor under you, the raised seat at the front. If you haven't, use the picture from today. Then notice the order in the room you're sitting in now. What's raised up? What gets the best seat? What does everything point toward? Don't change anything yet. Just see it, and rest with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
In the gurdwara. The Guru's door: no idols, no one seated higher than the Granth, and heads covered for all who enter. Today's word.
Your line: no one above the word. Today, in one room you're in, notice who gets the high seat, and choose the floor once. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, Sikhs and visitors remove their shoes, cover their heads, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib if they choose, and sit on the floor together; the Granth rests on a raised seat under a canopy.

original.note: Punjabi: the Guru's door, the place where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Granth sits high because it's a precious old book.
what it means: in the gurdwara no one and nothing is placed above the Guru's word: no idol, no raised seat, heads covered for all.
what a scholar hears: the code builds the hall's layout on one rule: the Granth is the Guru, so its seat is the only raised one.
recall: ten hymns of Guru Gobind Singh

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the gurdwara (no idols; no special seat in the Granth's presence; heads covered; open to all)

notes: The code's gurdwara rules are paraphrased: no idol/image worship in the gurdwara; sitting on a cushion or distinctive seat in the Granth's presence in the sangat is against gurmat; heads covered; any person of any country, religion or caste may visit. Please confirm each, and that 'heads covered for all' is a fair reading of the code.
'Gurdwara means the Guru's door' is given as the word's meaning, not an etymology; please confirm.
Current practice on chairs for elderly or disabled worshippers varies and is debated; the script does not raise it. A Keeper may wish to add a line.
'In some gurdwaras, a basket of head scarves' and 'shoes in rows on racks' are general descriptions; please confirm.
